speechtext: 1916 FIRE

maintopic: ANNIVERSARY OF 1916 FIRE-SIGNIFICANCE OF MACEUNVEILING OF PLAQUE COMMEMORATING VICTIMS OF FIRE
speechtext:
On this February 3, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians will recall the fire which destroyed the Centre Block of Parliament in 1916.
Not only did the blaze destroy a beautiful architectural structure, but seven Canadians also lost their lives, including a Member of Parliament. A new building was erected a few years later in which there was a plaque to honour the late Bowman Brown Law, the Hon. Member for Yarmouth. Regrettably there was no reference to the six other individuals who lost their lives in this fire.
This anomaly of history has lasted for 72 years. Earlier today, thanks to you, Mr. Speaker, the omission was finally
corrected and a fitting tribute was paid to the six Parliament employees who died in the 1916 blaze.

subsubtopic: ARBITRATION OF RAILWAY DISPUTE-CALL FOR PROMPT SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of 400 railway employees in my riding and the Sarnia area I would like to appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) not to extend the time limit allowed to the arbitrator in the labour dispute between the railway companies and the unions.
Although we commend the arbitrator for the interim wage increases granted today, these workers have been without a contract for over 18 months and are getting increasingly impatient with the process. The arbitration has already gone far beyond the 60 days originally intended and still the workers have received no indication of when a final settlement will be reached.
All the relevant information has been in the hands of the arbitrator for some time now, and the workers feel that any further delays will result in renegotiation, not arbitration. The railway workers want a settlement to be reached so that they can return to being concerned about railway services rather than contract disputes.

subsubtopic: NEW BRUNSWICK DOMTAR PLANT-PRESENCE OF DIOXINS IN NEIGHBOURING SEDIMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, dioxins are probably the most toxic substance ever unleashed on our planet. Thus it is extremely troubling to learn of the 20 years of complacency of federal authorities and New Brunswick provincial authorities with respect to dioxins found in the waters and sediment around the Domtar plant in the Miramichi Basin.

February 3, 1988
Fact: In 1970, the Fisheries and Forest Department wrote to Domtar to say that the waters affected were exceedingly toxic.
Fact: In 1981, Environment Canada published a report based on years of tests on dioxins in the sediment.
Fact: In 1987, Environment Canada wrote the province with further test results showing particularly dangerous toxins at 650 times the level of background concentrations.
Fact: Fisheries Canada considered charges but never followed through.
Fact: Agriculture Canada has never conducted a study on the effects on cattle which graze in the area and on the meat which is used locally.
Fact: The Domtar plant now wants to reopen although there is stored wood on the premises yet unprotected.
When will the federal Government take its responsibility for human health, agriculture, and fisheries seriously? When will it stop ignoring its own studies, and act?

subsubtopic: FUTURE OF HAWKER-SIDDELEY PLANT AT TRENTON, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March Hawker-Siddeley, the British owned multinational, announced it was going to sell or close its Trenton plant in central Nova Scotia. Closing this plant would virtually shut down the town and throw hundreds of workers onto the unemployment lines.
Shortly thereafter, Lavalin, the large multinational company from Montreal, came forward with a proposal to take over the plant. At that time federal officials gave the Lavalin proposal top marks. That was in mid 1987. Last fall the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) and the then President of the Treasury Board went to Trenton to announce that no buyer could be found and Ottawa would take on the job of finding one. They signed a contract with Hawker-Siddeley agreeing to act as the company's agent and sell the plant by April 2.
Over that period the plant would be kept open with Ottawa paying for any losses the company occurred. As part of the deal for Ottawa acting as a middleman, Hawker-Siddeley insisted and Ottawa agreed that any new owner not be allowed for a period of three years to lease railcars that it produces. According to the union officials, if the plant is only allowed to make railcars for sales, it would almost certainly fail again.
There is a glut of railcars on the market at the present time due to overproduction in the United States. Why has the Government agreed to such a deal? Why is it agreeing to the eventual shut-down of the Trenton industry?
Last November the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) visited Trenton and Pictou County. He told the workers his Government was working hard to find a buyer. Where is the action by this Government?

subsubtopic: AFGHANISTAN-CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF SOVIET TROOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Afghans throughout the world have been horrified and appalled to see their homeland torn apart, their families and friends killed, and their children maimed, in the course of eight years of brutal occupation of Afghanistan by Soviet troops. There are estimates that over 163,000 children between the ages of eight and 14 years have been kidnapped and sent to the Soviet Union for indoctrination. Despite all this, the Afghanistan fighting spirit has survived and will ultimately result in victory.
February 3, 1988

The Afghanistan Association of Ontario has demanded an immediate withdrawal of all Soviet troops in Afghanistan and the return of the kidnapped children to their grieving mothers. They ask the Government of Canada to officially recognize the Afghan Mujahadeen, to send humanitarian aid to the liberated areas of Afghanistan, and to apply effective political and economic pressures on the Soviet Union.
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to use these and all other means available to him to obtain an immediate withdrawal of Soviet troops from Afghanistan.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT FORECASTS MADE BY MEMBERS OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past number of months various polls have told us that the Opposition has followed the strategy of questioning the Government's credibility rather than its record or policies.
With the next budget statement one week away, it might be worth while to recall what some opposition Members said after the Economic Statement of November, 1984. The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) said: "They will destroy thousands of jobs. The effect of this program would be a net increase in unemployment". The Hon. Member for
Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) said: "As many as 100,000 people could lose their jobs". The former Member for Hamilton Mountain said: "Fifty thousand will become unemployed". The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said after the May, 1985, Budget: "There is a lack of job creation".
Here are the facts, Mr. Speaker. Over a million jobs have been created since that first statement. It is the credibility of the Opposition that Canadians should question.

speechtext:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REFERRAL BY HOUSE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the conflict of interest guidelines are, as I have acknowledged many times, the responsibility of the Prime Minister; and the integrity of the Government and all of its Members is also the responsibility of the Prime Minister.
I am as saddened, as I am sure any Member of the House is, or any Leader of any political Party, when any Member of his political Party, or any Member of the House, fails to comply, not only with the conflict of interest guidelines, but with any rules and regulations that govern our conduct. It is a serious problem in the 1980s, particularly conflict of interest, not only in this jurisdiction but in all jurisdictions.
I said this morning, and I have said in other circumstances, that I view the conflict of interest guidelines with the utmost of importance, and their enforcement will be with the utmost of severity.
I deeply regret, obviously, any breach, inadvertent or otherwise, of the guidelines, because the Canadian people are entitled to the observance of the highest standards. When those standards are lessened in any way, clearly this is unacceptable to me, and unacceptable to all Members of the House.
With regard to the conflict of interest guidelines, therefore, which are under my direct responsibility, when I was apprised, not of a violation, but of the possibility of a violation, which was not public knowledge in any way, I immediately instructed the officials of the Government to seek confirmation, and if confirmation was forthcoming, to provide it to me. When that was done, I immediately acted to seek the resignation of a Minister. It seems to me that that is in keeping with the most genuine spirit of parliamentary accountability and responsibility-
In regard to a separate matter, the administration of which law does not come under me but comes under an independent officer of Parliament, a parliamentary committee is presently considering this. The Minister of Energy has publicly stated that it would be his intention, at an appropriate time, to go before that committee and provide whatever testimony is required.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question of the Hon. Member who has had a substantial interest in this issue. Hon. Members will recall that one of the important conclusions of the Deschenes Commission, in light of the fact that it was not in a position to travel and hold hearings overseas or behind the Iron Curtain, was that there should be established safeguards with respect to the taking of evidence and the terms of investigations of alleged crimes. We as a Government, and I on behalf of the Government, accepted the recommendations of the Deschenes Commission.
We are in fact now negotiating with a variety of countries on both sides of the Iron Curtain to make sure that the Deschenes conditions are met, namely, the protection of reputations through confidentiality, the use of independent interpreters, access to original documents, access to witnesses' previous statements, freedom of examination of witnesses in agreement with Canadian rules of evidence, and the videotaping of such evidence.
We intend to make sure that Canadian standards of justice prevail with respect to prosecutions undertaken.

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-UNITED STATES' FUNDING OF NICARAGUAN CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. The Prime Minister will know that today could turn out to be either a very positive day or a very negative day for the peace process in Central America, depending on how the United States Congress responds to President Reagan's most recent request for funding for the Contras. The Prime Minister will also know of the profound disapproval of most Canadians for the approach of the United States Government in Central America.
Would the Prime Minister not take this opportunity, as the Prime Minister of Canada, on behalf of all Canadians, to say something today to the United States Congress about how much Canada would like it if the Congress turned down the President's proposal for further funding?

subsubtopic: FORMER MINISTER S STATEMENT RESPECTING RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, at the request of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), I handed in my resignation as Minister of Supply and Services. Today, I would like to explain here in the House the circumstances that led me to do so. The demands of political life in recent years, both on my family and on me personally, led me to ask an old friend for a personal loan, and he agreed.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear before the House that this circumstance never in any way placed me in a position where my interests conflicted with the ministerial duties that were mine in this Government. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, 1 can assure my colleagues in the House that the friend in question never received any favours or privileges in return.
However, I involuntarily neglected to declare this situation as required by the conflict of interest directives, thus contravening the spirit of the Ministers' code of conduct.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I sincerely regret this serious error of omission.
Mr. Prime Minister, obviously I sincerely regret the embarrassment I have caused the Government and you yourself, Prime Minister.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to say that it has been an honour and a privilege to serve as a Member of Cabinet, and 1 would like to thank my colleagues and all Members of this House who gave me their support when I was exercising my ministerial duties.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 also wish to thank my constituents in Langelier for their constant support, and I can assure them that I will continue to be a faithful defender of their interests, both here and in my riding.

Copyright Act
The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-60, an Act to amend the Copyright Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my duty to report to the House and rule with respect to the report stage of Bill C-60, an Act to amend the Copyright Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof. There are six motions on amendment on the Order Paper standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).

Motion No. 1 was moved in committee, debated at length and finally defeated. Therefore, pursuant to Standing Order 114(10), the motion will not be selected.

Motion No. 2 causes the Chair some difficulty. That part of Motion No. 2 which is lettered "e" was moved, debated and then withdrawn in committee. In addition, the Chair is of the opinion that the whole motion goes beyond the scope of the clause and the Bill which it attempts to improve upon. This is not in order. May I refer the Hon. Member to Beauchesne's, Fifth Edition, Citation 773, and to May, Twentieth Edition, page 555.
I would also like to refer the Hon. Member to page 308 of the Selected Decisions of Speaker Lamoureux where it is clearly stated that a "-proposed amendment must be relevant-(and) can amplify aspects of a motion but cannot expand its scope." Thus I will not put Motion No. 2 to the House.

Motion Nos. 3 and 4 are acceptable and will be debated and voted on separately.

Motions No. 5 and 6 are somewhat similar. A motion exactly the same as Motion No. 6 was moved, debated and voted on in the negative in committee. Thus Motion No. 6 will not be selected.
Motion No. 5, while similar, is varied enough for the Chair to give the Hon. Member the benefit of the doubt. Thus Motion No. 5 will be debated and voted on separately.

The House will now proceed to the consideration of Motion No. 3.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Obviously, I accept your ruling. I hope that, notwithstanding, Your Honour will relax the rules of relevance, allowing me in my remarks to address what I consider to be the serious deficiencies in this Bill that my motion on ephemeral recordings for broadcasters and spontaneous rights for educators would have alleviated. This view is held by many Canadians. I would appreciate Your Honour's consideration in that regard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Motion No. 3
That Bill C-60, be amended in Clause 13 by striking out lines 39 to 48 at
page 14 and lines 1 to 19 at page 15 and substituting the following therefor:
"13. Subsections 50( 1) to (10) of the said Act are repealed."
She said: Mr. Speaker, with respect to my amendment which addresses Clause 13, Section 50(7), I would point out that this is an obsolete measure. It has never worked. Those who use the music in a public place or in a retail outlet are essentially commercial users who are accruing benefits, income, and in a sense depriving the creators of those lovely sounds coming across the airwaves of their just and due economic rights. That is what this Bill is all about. It deals with copyright which would affect and bring economic rights to creators in our society.
If the intention of Bill C-60 is to provide economic benefit to creators, the retention of Section 50(7) in the Act is inconsistent with the goals of the Bill. Therefore it should be removed. It is also very inconsistent when the Chair has had to rule that my amendments are beyond the scope of the Bill. I suggest that while the Government and, obviously, Ministers have the right, which I willingly accept and argued vigorously about with the Table Officers, they have avoided addressing some
February 3, 1988

very serious matters. At the same time they have shown incredible inconsistency by retaining an issue that is an exemption. After wiping out the entire Section 50(1) through (10) they have decided to keep one single clause, which is the exemption clause. That makes absolutely no sense.
The section has been judicially interpreted to exempt also public performances by means of juke boxes or similar devices where the user pays a fee to obtain the performance. The exemption does not include wired music systems where the music originates with a phonograph in one location and is distributed by wire or other means to speakers placed in another location or locations. Since the section refers to "gramophone" and "radio receiving set" it presently may not extend to performances produced by tape recorders or television.
The Liberal Government White Paper entitled From Gutenberg to Telidon in 1984, which was a consultation paper, and the Conservative Government's subcommittee study on the revision of copyright entitled The Charter of Rights For Creators in 1985, and the Conservative Government's response, recommended that this exemption be abolished. How can the Government say that it is not dealing with exemptions and not dealing with fair dealing in this Bill and then move to retain an exemption with regard to fair dealing and abolish the rest of that particular article? It makes no logic or sense.
The other aspect of this is that it is an obsolete clause. It is one that has never been used. The advocacy for its abolition has been constant and continuous. I am not allowed to talk about ephemeral recordings which relate to an act that takes place on a daily basis in this country through broadcasters having to tape in order that they can show the recording at a different hour in another part of the country. This is going to be found to be illegal and they might well have court sanctions. Playing a record outside or on a tape recorder in a discotheque where youths come to be entertained will be kept as an exception that does not have to be paid for. It is so illogical as to blow the mind.
The legislative committee when studying Bill C-60 heard strong advocacy for the abolition of this section from PROCAN and CAPAC. They expressed their absolute astonishment over the retention of this exemption, and stressed that there should be no exceptions to the public performance right for musical works, not even for educational or religious purposes.
In this regard, I think that they have spoken strongly. From my perspective the exemption is totally out of context with what we are dealing with. Here we are talking about a small, fairly insignificant article that no one has asked to be kept. Because it is outside of the parameters of this Bill, users of the service have been refused spontaneous rights in order that our children can have up-to-date information. We would not
Copyright Act
deprive any creator from proper remuneration for their work. But we wish to enable our children to have the latest and most up-to-date information, whether it is by photocopying an article or an editorial from the paper yesterday, and then collecting later and negotiating with the copyright board, or whether the teacher has decided that the issues on free trade, or the issues on apartheid, or what is happening in the Middle East are so current and important that the teacher cannot wait for that information to be listed with the collective in order to negotiate a fair price. The whole approach is ludicrous, and I cannot make head or tail out of the Government's approach.
I would like very much to recommend that Bill C-60 be amended in Clause 13 by striking out lines 39 to 48 at page 14 and lines 1 to 19 at page 15 and substituting the following therefor: "13. Subsections 50(1) to (10) of the said Act are repealed."
It is inconsistent with the supposed philosophy of the Government. It does not meet with the Government's phase one and phase two which were supposed to come in together in order that we could see the impact after we had dealt with fair dealings and exemptions, and here we keep an exemption. Either we want to deal with exemptions, or we do not want to deal with exemptions. If we are not going to deal with exemptions and fair dealings, then let us take them out. If we are going to allow fair dealings and exemptions, then for goodness' sakes let us at least allow spontaneous work used by teachers and ephemeral recordings used by the CBC in order that the CRTC regulations are met, and a proper tape kept of music so that we can have the finest sound and not ruin the intent of the artist when presented to the public. We are totally inconsistent. It is a poor Bill. It has been badly thought through, and the Minister has been very poorly advised.
1 would call for a movement to accept this particular amendment.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party I am pleased to be able to respond to Motion No. 3. While I seconded the motion put forward by my hon. friend, I must say that I did it to enable us to debate this particular amendment. At this point our plan is to oppose the amendment, and I wish to explain why.
As my hon. friend has indicated, this amendment is designed to repeal an existing exemption. The exemption is commonly known as the "gramophone" or "juke-box" amendment. This exemption frees the users of record players and juke boxes from paying royalties to the owners of the copyright in works that are publicly performed.
If one took the extreme position that, if the exemption is removed as has been proposed, some small users, for example, a corner store owner, who incidentally may be playing the radio during business hours, would technically be in breach of the law. For that reason, we find this to be a peculiar amendment.

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
1 wish to remind Members that the publication entitled The Charter of Rights for Creators, published in October, 1985, contained the following recommendation:
44. The revised law should contain an exception from copyright liability for performances of protected works by means of radios, television sets and playback machines that incidentally take place in public.
The Charter of Rights for Creators acknowledged this problem when it stated:
Clearly it would be an improper extension of copyright law if these
essentially private uses were, even in theory, considered copyright infringements.
While the subcommittee called for the removal of the existing exemption, it also recommended that the revised law should contain an exemption from copyright liability for performances of protected works by means of radios, television sets, and playback machines that incidentally take place in public. I realize that I am reiterating that point to make it clear that it is obvious that this motion ought not to be supported. 1 believe that this is a reasonable approach which, quite frankly, would make the revised law workable.
I would like to suggest to my hon. colleague that exemptions will be considered in phase two of the revision of this Act. During the committee hearings, the Minister made a rather vague commitment that phase two would be addressed in the spring. At that time Members of my Party pressed the Minister to expedite that process. I am optimistic that the need for it is so obvious that at phase two the Minister will bring forward the appropriate initiative.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), and the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). The points that have been discussed here today were discussed at length in the legislative committee.
I think it is important to look at proposed Section 50.7 in respect of the totality of the Bill. If it is looked at in that context, Bill C-60 repeals Sections 50.1 to 50.10 of the present Copyright Act which deal with the copyright appeal board. However, proposed Section 50.7 is being reintroduced slightly modified to reflect the wording of the Bill. Proposed Section
50.7	deals with the copyright appeal board's power over the fees, charges, or royalties collectible from the owner of a radio receiving set or gramophone. Basically, proposed subsection
50.7	provides that the board cannot establish fees where there is a public performance by means of any radio receiving set or gramophone in any place other than the theatre that is ordinarily and regularly used for entertainment and to which there is an admission charge. Thus proposed subsection 50.7 is an exception, an exception from the payment of copyright royalties.
As I mentioned earlier, the intention of Bill C-60 is to deal with certain issues, as has been mentioned. It does not deal with exceptions. All exceptions will be dealt with together in the next phase of the copyright revision.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, I would submit that this amendment is not appropriate for Bill C-60.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. May I change the name of the seconder from the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), with his consent, to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Clause 24 of the Bill reads:
Subsection 46(1) and section 46.1 of the Copyright Act, as enacted by
section 11, apply in respect of any alleged infringement of copyright occurring
prior to, on or after the day on which section 11 comes into force.
Clause 11 of the Bill amends the section which deals with utilitarian or functional items. They will no longer be considered eligible for copyright protection. The section would have a retroactive effect by virtue of Clause 24.
I do not know what advice the Minister obtained, but I am sure that she, her Government, and her Party would not particularly care to be perceived as stripping businessmen of their acquired right, for the Government is prejudicing its case, or stripping them of a cause of action under existing law. The Minister should have known-and if she did not know, her
February 3, 1988

advisers should have told her-that it is a basic tenet of the law that they cannot retroactively make what was legal illegal. I think this is fundamental to democracy and fundamental to fairness. Attention should be paid to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, probably Section 7. We have already had one surprise, a delightful, well reasoned, and very welcomed decision by the Supreme Court of Canada. I would hope that we would not have to go that same route in order for businessmen to have justice of the day.
What we have here is a potential for criminal sanctions as well as civil sanctions, starting at $25,000 and running up to $1 million. One could go to jail for six months or up to five years. We are not playing Monopoly-"Go to jail, do not pass Go, do not collect $200". This is a serious infringement. It is a very serious matter. I just wonder how carefully they looked at the whole issue, because they wanted to do it in two phases.
1 will read into the record the very enlightening remarks of major corporations in the country which appeared before us. They showed us what a very badly conceived Bill it was, how poorly written it was, and how full of errors, both linguistic and content-wise, it was. I started to count the number of changes and found that it was in the hundreds. It was a very sloppily drafted Bill. I cannot say that it was hurried, because they had three years in which they thought about it. I do not think careful thought was given to this section.
My amendment would ensure that we are not prejudicing the cause of businessmen. It becomes prospective, not retroactive, because a cause of action should receive a clear judgment in the courts.
If we really want to be fair in this matter, there will be little damage if the amendment is accepted because there is a limitation on copyright. I do not suggest that 1 am an expert in this field, but I have certainly tried to become informed. What I know is that copyright infringement falls after three years. Therefore, in accepting this amendment we would be protecting those who were in litigation, those who are presently in litigation, and those who just might go to litigation because they are unaware of what is happening with Bill C-60. They might choose to go to litigation over the next three years. We would really be grandfathering the rights of these people under the existing law. The courts should decide and legal counsel should argue. We would pay a very small price so that people in business, those who have worked painstakingly at their designs, will not have unfair competition, pirating of their works, or counterfeiting of their designs.
I urge the Minister to consider this motion very seriously, not to turn it down strictly because it has come from the Opposition. A basic tenet of the law-and this is fundamental to democracy and fairness-should not be subject to retroactivity.
Let me read into the record what the bar associations have said. I think it is vital to know what is the thinking out there. First, Ogilvy, Renault indicates the following:
Copyright Act
The retroactivity-that is created under this clause is without precedent and unconscionable. It is clear under the current law that a cause of action for infringement exists in relation to the copying of a functional article, and in many instances parties have relied on the existing law to commence proceedings. To abolish Clause 11 retroactively will unfairly expose these persons to damages and costs. This clause must be deleted.
Second, Riches indicates:
It is inappropriate for proposed section 46.1 to apply retroactively. Persons have governed their affairs on the basis of the law as it now stands. To change retroactively existing rights and liabilities by means of legislation is objectionable. Proposed subsections 46(2) and (3) are not subject to retroactive application; nor should proposed section 46.1.
Further to that, Balmer indicates:
Clause 11 should not operate retrospectively so as to deprive copyright holders of claims to copyright which existed prior to the Bill's coming into force.
The last one is from Cassels, and I should like to read it into the record to show the Government how unfairly and inappropriately it is treating businessmen. It reads:
Our clients, 554072 Ontario Inc. and Wheel Tronic Inc., commenced an action for copyright infringement in 1985 against the defendants who through a process of "reverse engineering" copied our clients' unique design for an automotive hoist and jack beam. If Clause 24 is adopted, our clients may be deprived of the cause of action which they have been pursuing at great expense, both in terms of money and time, for the past two and one half years.
It is now three years. It continues:
On their behalf, we urge that Clause 11 be made prospective only, or, alternatively, that a provision be added to avoid the prejudice which would otherwise be caused to our clients and to others who may be involved in similar proceedings.
1 suggest that under the Charter of Rights this is illegal. It will make money for lawyers and result in misery and costs for businessmen. It is not consistent with the philosophy of law, and I think that the Minister should withdraw it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to respond to Motion No. 4. I do not know whether I seconded the motion in the end, but certainly it was my intention because I support the motion very enthusiastically on behalf of the New Democratic Party.
As the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) indicated, this amendment is designed to remove the retroactivity clause. I cannot imagine a Member of this House who would support a retroactivity clause. I remember debates vividly especially when the National Energy Program was introduced which had an element of retroactivity. I recall day after day, nay, week after week, when Members would be rising indicating how abhorrent this type of an initiative was and how, as Members of Parliament, we ought not to be introducing retroactive legislation. We certainly supported that notion in many respects.
When a firm, a business, a corporation or an individual makes plans and commits itself financially, not only in capital but in human resources, to carry out a particular plan, be it a business plan or some other type of plan, so much depends

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
upon their ability to carry that out step by step. When Bill C-60 was being considered actively by the legislative committee, various companies made it very clear that retroactivity would cause them very serious problems. The problematic nature of the retroactivity clause was something that they brought to our attention because of the very negative impact that would accrue to them and on the enterprises they represented.
There is another side to this matter worth sharing, namely, the legal opinion. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, have always been concerned about the legality of various pieces of legislation to ensure that they not only follow the spirit of the law but the law itself. I want to say that the retroactivity of Clause 11 created under this clause is without precedent and is certainly highly unconscionable. It is clear under current law that a cause of action for infringement exists in relation to the copying of a functional article and, in many instances, parties have relied on the existing law to commence proceedings. To abolish Clause 11 retroactively will unfairly expose those persons to damages and to costs. Therefore, 1 believe this clause ought to be deleted.
I might add that I believe it is inappropriate for proposed Section 46(1) to apply retroactively. Persons have governed their affairs on the basis of the law as it now stands. The point I was attempting to make earlier and to change retroactively existing rights and liabilities by means of legislation is something that I think most people would find to be objectionable. Proposed subsections 26(2) and 26(3) are not subject to retroactive application, nor should proposed Section 46(1).
Clause 11 should not operate retroactively so as to deprive copyright holders of claims to copyright which existed prior to this Bill coming into force.
It is also useful to point out that as currently worded this clause does not refer to Section 46(2). 1 think that is something you would have noted in your examination. There is no reference to Section 46(2), Mr. Speaker. Therefore, we are in total support of this exclusion. In no event should Section 46(2) be made retroactive as this could possibly affect certain ongoing litigation.
What I have said is perfectly obvious in terms of what must be done and what must not be done. Therefore, on behalf of my Party, may I say that we plan to support this amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is to make the industrial design section in Bill C-60 apply only in the future and not retroactively.
Until two or three years ago no one thought copyright extended to purely functional articles, such as tailpipes. But court cases decided that copyright could apply to functional articles. This created a legal authority for other court cases which argued that copyright was being infringed by copying purely functional articles, like the hull of a boat. This legal result was never intended.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Bar Association agreed that copyright should not extend to functional articles like boats and tailpipes. Bill C-60 reflects this view. Bill C-60 says that copyright does not and never did extend to functional articles. Bill C-60 clarifies the law not only for the future but also for the past. Copyright was never intended and did not apply to functional articles.
Bill C-60 sets out the division between what is protected by copyright and what is protected by industrial design. One of the ways this is done is by providing that copyright never did apply to purely functional articles. This is what Clause 24 says. If Clause 24 is amended as suggested by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) then Bill C-60 would say that in future copyright will not apply to functional articles. However, the state of the law before Bill C-60 will be based on the recent court cases which extended copyright to functional articles, and that is a result which was never intended.
To avoid this unintended result, Clause 24 of Bill C-60 states what the law was always intended to say, that copyright does not extend to purely functional articles. For that reason, the Government cannot accept the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal.

speechtext:
Concerning the Speaker's ruling, may I read into the record exactly what has happened here.
Motion Nos. 5 and 6 are somewhat similar. A motion exactly the same as Motion No. 6 was moved, debated and voted on in the negative in committee. Thus Motion No. 6 will not be selected. Motion No. 5, while similar, is varied enough
February 3, 1988

for the Chair to give the Hon. Member the benefit of the doubt. Thus Motion No. 5 will be debated and voted on separately.

Motion No. 5
That Bill C-60 be amended by adding, immediately after line 46 at page 22, the following:
"26. (1) Five years after the coming into force of this Act, and at the end of every three-year period thereafter, a comprehensive review of the provisions and operation of this Act, including the effect of such provisions, shall be undertaken by such joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, as may be designated or established for that purpose.
(2) Within six months after the completion of the review referred to in subsection (1), the joint committee so designated or established for that purpose shall submit a report to Parliament on its findings, including any changes the committee would recommend."
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is really a sad day when we are looking at a very serious Bill which obviously has not captivated the enthusiastic understanding or involvement of many Members of this House. Quite rightly so because it is an extraordinarily complex Bill. It is one that I found difficult to work with and I think most Members were not exactly enthralled with the many, many hundreds of hours that we spent trying to find some rational and fair answers that would meet the needs of the users as well as the creators.
In trying to arrive at some kind of fairness in our system and in trying to accord economic rights, which are due to the creators, we have embarked on some new and exciting undertakings. From the time of the White Paper, which was called From Gutenberg to Telidon, through to the study undertaken in 1985, which resulted in The Charter of Rights for Creators, that balance, that tenuous balance between the user and the creator resulted in the initiation of some very new and avant garde ideas to improve the economic opportunities of the creators to revamp this very old Bill, a Bill designed for other uses. In so doing, we must be able to ensure that all this innovation that is being brought in in a patchwork way between phases one and two of the Bill is reviewed. It is in that light that I wish to include a sunset clause in Bill C-60. We would then be in a position to review legislation that has been highly controversial. If we review the legislation in five years, we will have had five years of experience with a variety of its clauses. We would be able to assess the impact of public exhibition rights on curators.
To our knowledge, no other country has public exhibition rights. I think they might be exciting but might create serious problems. I would like to have that assessed and I would like to assess the efficiency of the new thrust. 1 would like to be able to assess the potential problems which might arise as a result of the fair dealings or exemptions which we still have not seen and will come forward in phase two in which I hope a similar provision will be included.
Copyright Act
How can we assess what is happening with collectives if they have not yet been implemented? Many of the provincial Governments have serious reservations about these collectives. The Minister received a letter from the Minister of Culture and Communications of Ontario who expressed some of her serious reservations, as have two other provincial Ministers. Collectives and negotiations are not in place yet and there are serious concerns as to how this will actually operate.
How will we know if, under its newly constituted mandate, a copyright board is large enough to meet the demands and will be efficient and able to fulfil its mandate under the law? As collectives are a fairly new concept, particularly in some areas of jurisdiction, will the board be able to work effectively with the collectives? Will negotiations be undertaken in a way that will meet the goals of this Bill?
All Hon. Members, and certainly the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) should be well aware that technology requires upgrading. We do not want to leave this Bill alone for another 60 years. We want to be able to ensure that the Bill is working in balance with the interests of the curators and the users, not just to the benefit of the legal profession, causing it to create unnecessary legislation and tie-ups in the courts.
The Minister of Culture and Communications of Ontario, Lily Munro, wrote the Minister of Communications and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) about Bill C-60. She indicates in a letter that her colleagues and she are carefully reviewing the proposals and would want to provide some comments in the future. Referring to the public exhibition rights, she said in the third paragraph of her letter, the following:
-we feel that the possible implications of this amendment have not been fully assessed and may be too far reaching. Art galleries and museums not only have a role in providing public access to creative works but also, in many cases, have educational objectives to which they must adhere.
Interpretation of collections is an essential part of the curatorial responsibility of such institutions and provides an educational experience for the viewer, particularly in a historical context. The introduction of an exhibition right as stated in Bill C-60, would alter this historically established balance between creators and the institution.
She went on to say:
I am very supportive of initiatives that improve the economic situation of artists and I believe that galleries and museums in Ontario share this objective.
Certainly we heard that they did so throughout the course of our hearings. She went on:
The exhibition right as currently drafted may act, however, as a disincentive not only to museums and galleries, but also to corporations and other individuals to purchase, lend or donate contemporary art.
The Minister went on to say:
-there has not been sufficient analysis and discussion among the affected parties to clarify the real intention of this section and the practical implementation of those intentions.
She concluded by saying:
I strongly recommend that the addition of an "exhibition right" be reserved pending much fuller investigation and consultation on the issues, options and

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
effects it may have on indigenous contemporary art and the public exhibition community. 1 urge you to review this amendment-
There seems to be much glasnost between the federal and provincial Governments. We are all so happy and Meech Lake is a marvellous undertaking. Everyone is cosy and lovey-dovey. If everyone is so happy, then the Minister should have taken into consideration the need for much more careful and considered communications and consultations before bringing in a brand new right of this kind. She should also have assured herself that mechanisms were in place for the collectives and were ready to roll. Neither of these things was done.
I would like to bring one last point to the attention of the House. The Minister, in answering my concerns, told me that we could not bind future Parliaments. When I introduced a similar amendment, the Minister answered, I suppose because she was not well informed, in the the following way:
Could I just perhaps comment before Mrs. Finestone leaves. The difficulty that I think anyone would have with this particular proposal, even though I agree wholeheartedly with the need to be able to force governments to move on issues like this, is it really is not acceptable for one Parliament to try to bind another Parliament.
I went on to advise the Minister that we had done so in other instances. The Minister then said:
The Parliament, regardless of the government-but for one Parliament to try to say this is what you must do . .. Now there may be ways that we can see that reviews are carried out, but it is not feasible to do that, and that is why-
I interrupted and brought to her attention that she herself had brought an amendment like this before the House and that there were two other instances of it in the last couple of years. One such instance was the access to information legislation and the other was under a workplace hazardous materials information Act.
I would like to remind the Minister that when she was the Minister of Employment and Immigration and brought Bill C-62 before the House, she moved the adoption of a very similar amendment. In that Bill, she wanted the following clause adopted:
Five years after the coming into force of this Act, and at the end of every three-year period thereafter, a comprehensive review of the provisions and operation of this Act, including the effect of such provisions, shall be undertaken by such joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, as may be designated or established for that purpose.
(2) Within six months after the completion of the review referred to in subsection (1), the joint committee so designated or established for that purpose shall submit a report to Parliament on its findings, including any changes the committee would recommend."
I did not even think of putting in my motion the part about a review at the end of every three-year period thereafter. I suppose when the Minister responded to me in committee and caused the rejection of this proposal, she forgot that she had done it herself. She forgot that her colleagues had done it in two other Bills. 1 would like to remind the Hon. Minister and her advisers that they did do this and suggest that they accept this amendment. I believe the sunset clause is well suited to this particular Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having a chance to make some comments following those of my hon. friend, the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), who has once again presented a most convincing case for the introduction of a sunset clause into the process as a result of Motion No. 5. The New Democratic Party will be supporting this initiative. I think it is very appropriate.
The Member has made the case that incorporating a sunset clause into the legislation is not a new idea. A number of precedents for this exist. I recall that with regard to the Access to Information Act the feeling was that a regular review would be appropriate to ensure that Members of Parliament and the public have access to appropriate information in order to keep the Government on the straight and narrow.
The Member for Mount Royal indicated as well that the workplace hazardous materials information Act has a built in review process as does the employment equity Bill and the very famous Bank Act. There are other cases in which a regular review is considered to be not only appropriate but absolutely necessary. This has become necessary largely due to the technological changes which are occurring in so many fields today, particularly in the arts, which require a periodic review of this type of copyright legislation. The sunset clause allows for that.
If we want meaningful and responsive copyright legislation the need for periodic review becomes obvious. We do not want to have the previous situation repeated. In the past, present members of the Government called for changes to the Copyright Act time after time and the Government of the day kept dragging its feet. Nevertheless, wc have today made a whole set of extremely complex changes.
1 must admit that I do not understand the implications of them all. I have studied them adequately to be aware of most of them, but it is an extremely complex area with dramatic changes taking place in technology, production, and marketing. It is, therefore, very appropriate that we are now revising this copyright legislation. It has been nearly 60 years since this legislation has received the examination which it has during the last number of months. This review was certainly long overdue.
The Keyes-Brunet report of 1977 recommended that provision be made for the periodic revision of copyright law. It may be useful to remind Members of one of the critical recommendations of that report. The title of that report was Copyright in Canada: Proposals for Revision of the Law. It made four recommendations, the first being:
That continuous evaluation be maintained of the impact of existing and
emerging intellectual property systems.
The need for that recommendation is perfectly clear. The second recommendation was:
That provision be made for a means to conduct and maintain a continuing
review and study of copyright law and practice, and of technological and other
February 3, 1988

developments in the field, with a view to encouraging the initiation and
development of policy recommendations.
This seminal report on the need to change the Copyright Act pointed out the necessity for an ongoing periodic review of any legislation dealing with copyright. The third recommendation was:
That provision be made for the periodic revision of copyright law.
That is straightforward enough. The fourth recommendation was:
That a mechanism be provided to initiate and conduct regular liaison,
consultation and discussion with private and public copyright interests in
Canada, and with foreign copyright offices and international organizations.
It is most important that in addition to a review process being automatically triggered as a result of the sunset clause appropriate extensive and intensive consultations take place with all organizations interested and involved in a direct way in copyright legislation, whether they be users or creators. We support this, Mr. Speaker.
The past Chairman of the Standing Committee on Communications, who is from Edmonton, expressed sympathy for the notion of sunset clauses during the legislative hearings. He said "Philosophically I rather favour sunsets". I suppose that he was not necessarily referring to Alberta sunsets which are, of course, magnificent, but to sunset clauses. That was the context of his comment.
With regard to identifying critical persons who have indicated their support for sunset clauses, as the Member for Mount Royal so adequately pointed out, the Minister herself indicated some time ago the need for a periodic review. This motion now makes that possible.
I know that the Parliamentary Secretary will likely be standing in a moment to express his views on Motion No. 5. I would like to put a query to him to which he may respond when he gets to his feet. I am sure that he has, as have most of us, received letters and visits from constituents, most of whom tend to be teachers, students, and librarians, who express concerns about various aspects of this copyright legislation.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Clinch) will use this opportunity to clarify what this means to those people in the learning and instructional fields who occasionally make use of copyright material to assist in demonstrating various points. If the Parliamentary Secretary would explain this, it would alleviate a lot of the concerns which I know from previous discussions are unnecessary and would enable Members to send to those making inquiries the actual words of the Hon. Member on this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I was not prepared to respond to the request of the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) with regard to questions from teachers and librarians, I would be more than willing to give a personal view of that in my position as a former teacher and member of the teaching community in Bathurst, New Brunswick for many years. I am sure there are many teachers and librarians there who are interested in the effects of the Bill.
The clauses in Motions Nos. 5 and 6 require mandatory review of legislation. Such clauses have been referred to as sunset clauses by members of the Opposition. Their inclusion suggest that some difficulties or unforeseen consequences are anticipated in the operation of a new piece of legislation. The purpose of a sunset clause is to guarantee a forum in which a public review must take place periodically.
In legislative committee, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) proposed a sunset clause for Bill C-60, stating that the new Hazardous Products Act and the Access to Information Act contained such clauses and that they set precedents for introducing one in the Copyright Act.

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
I suggest that each statute must be examined on its own merit. The provision of a statute in one case cannot be looked at in isolation. It must be examined within the context of the entire Act.
Take, for example, the new Flazardous Products Act, which comes into force in October of this year.
The Act provides for mandatory review two years after the coming into force of its Section 12, which refers to certain hazardous products, explosives, atomic materials, hazardous wastes and tobacco products.
Because of a feeling of urgency, the Bill was passed eight days after its introduction on June 22, 1987. Not all hazardous products were included or adequately defined. For example, the term "hazardous wastes" is not defined consistently in different statutes which deal with them.
It is clear that in this case the function of the review clause is not really to review the Bill but to complete it. This is not the case for the new copyright legislation. It will be completed in phase two, making a review clause unnecessary.
Another example of a sunset clause is in the Access to Information Act. Section 75 of the Act provides for its review within three years of its coming into force. This was introduced for a basic reason; access to information is a new concept, quite different from other statutes.
The first review of that Act took place last year. In its report, the committee suggested another review. The committee's report stated that a major reason for scheduling another review is that it is relatively new legislation. The report states that there has not been enough experience yet in a number of areas to determine satisfactorily whether both the structure and the provisions of the Act are adequate.
This is not the case with copyright legislation. Copyright legislation is not new, either on the domestic or on the international scene. The present law has been in force for 64 years, since 1924. Indeed, most countries in the world now have copyright legislation. There are two international copyright conventions to which most countries in the world belong. Many studies have preceded the preparation of the new Canadian copyright law, and international precedent was taken into full consideration.
Let me respond to the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap with regard to copyright in the teaching profession. In my opinion, the present copyright law, which has been in effect since 1924 prevents most of that which may happen in a classroom where teachers utilize materials and copy them without receiving permission. This law proposes to allow the creators and writers to receive some remuneration for their works. No one in the teaching profession disagrees with that.
There are two ways for this to work practically. One is to use the collective system, which is very familiar to Members from Quebec where that system is now in place. Assuming that we are talking about education, the department of education of
a province would belong to a collective and any artist or creator who belongs to that collective would be listed with the department. The department of education would pay a fee in order that anyone in the classroom could use the works of those artists or creators.
The other alternative in the discussion of exemptions or exceptions to the Copyright Act is to deal with these exceptions, and they will be dealt with in phase two of the Bill. Those groups who have expressed a concern are asking to be considered in the exceptions or exemptions to the Copyright Act. Those are the possibilities with respect to the practical implementation of the Bill. I hope I have answered my hon. friend's question adequately, as well as that of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Motion No. 5 in the name of my distinguished colleague, the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). I want to congratulate her for her participation in this issue and for the immense contribution she has made to the debate.
This motion which she has proposed is not only in order but quite logical. The Parliamentary Secretary indicated to us that one of the rationales for a sunset clause is to take into account legislation that is brand new, innovative or unprecedented.
The Hon. Member said that the copyright legislation does not fit into that category. I disagree with him. It is quite true that we have had copyright legislation in this country for a long time, but we should remember that it has not been reviewed for many years. Therefore, any new legislation introduced is a brand new concept.
Second, there are portions of the Bill which are clearly unprecedented not only in this country but everywhere that I can imagine. For example, the issue of exhibition rights is a brand new concept. I understand that it does not exist in the United States and has not existed here.
I know that my colleague from Mount Royal has expressed reservations about this particular clause because we simply do not know what will happen in a few years' time. Therefore, why not have a sunset clause by which we can review the exhibition rights and other pertinent issues that did not exist before the introduction of Bill C-60?
It is not only the Official Opposition that expresses this view. The Minister of Culture and Communications for Ontario, Lily Munro, stated in a letter dated December 11, 1987:
After consultation with many of the groups that would be affected by the introduction of an exhibition right, we feel that the possible implications of this amendment have not been fully assessed and may be too far reaching. Art galleries and museums not only have a role in providing public access to creative works but also, in many cases, have educational objectives to which they must adhere.
Interpretation of collections is an essential part of the curatorial responsibility of such institutions and provides an educational experience for the viewer, particularly in a historical context. The introduction of an exhibition right as
February 3, 1988

stated in Bill C-60, would alter this historically established balance between creators and the institution.
Of course, there is the whole issue of whether there would be a reluctance on the part of certain potential acquirers of art to obtain a particular piece of art if they knew, for instance, that the exhibition rights were not relinquished at the time of purchase. We do not know the answer to all these questions, and they are very important. That is why the suggestion made by the Hon. Member to include a sunset clause in this Bill is indeed quite appropriate.
There is also the question of the exhibition rights in the Bill as they pertain to another issue which is very close and dear to the hearts of certain Conservative Members of Parliament. That is the issue-and it is not my issue, I must say-of the so-called property rights that Conservatives like to bring to our attention every now and then, the firm belief of some Members of this House that once you purchase property it is yours and that is the end of it. I refer, for instance, to the debates of the House of Commons on October 15, 1987, in which the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) spoke. He talked about the lack of property rights as a regrettable omission and that the principle of freedom to pursue the gaining of a livelihood with respect to the Charter is diminished if one's freedom to simply keep, sell or buy is not secure. He said: "All this is simple common sense". How could the Hon. Member for Kitchener accept that this new concept of exhibition rights would be in legislation without a review process so that he could assure himself that there is no interference with that sacred principle he feels is so important, namely, the acquisition of property rights for Canadians?
Those are all very important issues to Conservative backbenchers who are bent upon this property rights thing, for Members of Parliament generally, and even for our provincial Governments. I know the Parliamentary Secretary is paying close attention to my remarks as I look across the floor. I know he will want to respond to this question in a very positive manner.
On December 4, 1987, with respect to the property rights issue which is so important to some Conservative Members-and I am sure because of this they will want to support the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal-the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) stated at page 11514 of Hansard:
Ownership is conducive to an individual's independence, freedom, and happiness. A man's house is his castle. However, what happens when he does not have the right to own that castle? From earliest times property has been defended. Aristotle expressed a strong defence of property and advanced the idea that private property is ordained by natural law and that ownership is conducive to progress.
According to this famous philosopher, ownership of property promotes the growth of character because two important virtues result from it-self control and liberty.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that not only opposition Members have concerns about the Bill. Indeed, Conservative
Copyright Act
Members have expressed the point that it is important to have a review mechanism such as the one offered to us by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal.
