Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak at third reading of this Bill, and its

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
amendments. 1 am very dissatisfied that two of my amendments did not receive Government understanding, which I think is highly regrettable in the present circumstances. 1 think the Government will rue the day it caused business people very serious financial loss. However, that is the Government's problem, not ours.
Copyright law is the legal expression of the rights granted to a creator to protect his or her work against a variety of unauthorized uses. That protection arises when a work is created by our artists and provides the legal foundation for the publishing, broadcasting, film, sound recording and other copyright based industries. Essentially, copyright law sets the rules under which market forces determine what music is heard, what records are made, what films are seen, what books are published and what programs are viewed on television, all here in Canada. Copyright law dates back to 1832 in a statute of the Legislature of Lower Canada. The British North America Act of 1867 placed exclusive jurisdiction concerning copyright with the federal Government. Several Acts were subsequently passed, culminating in the present 1924 Act which repealed all prior legislation-and, please note, all prior legislation. It did not do a patchwork job.
The 1924 Act provides that no person is entitled to copyright, or any similar right in respect of protected material except in accordance with the Act. It should be noted that this 1924 legislation was written during a period when there were no television sets. Can any Members remember when there were no television sets, no tape recorders, no VCRs and, Mr. Speaker, when adding machines were considered computers? As a result of these technological changes, copyright has changed considerably from being only the right to copy. Today works acquire value not only by means of reproduction of copies but through public performance and broadcasting.
Copyright law attempts to strike a balance between the competing interests of creators in exploiting their works and of the public interest in having access to those works. These things enrich our lives in many ways. Therefore the law grants creators important moral and economic rights.
The law also recognizes uses of works that are permitted without the authorization of the creator or the payment of royalties. Therefore copyright must concern itself with first providing creators' rights and then with the limiting of those rights. 1 would suggest that the quality of our cultural rights is dependent upon copyright. The subcommittee which looked at the revision of copyright in 1985 was told:
The quality of cultural life depends upon a country's intellectual and artistic creations and, to some extent, is a reflection of the encouragement and protection provided to creators. Copyright legislation can be regarded as a means of encouraging creative and intellectual activity in providing adequate protection to creators, entrepreneurs, and the cultural industries, in the creation, development and exploitation of the products of creativity, and the arts in general.
I do not know of anyone in the House who would debate that point. However, I do not believe that it is the saviour of our cultural life to the extent that the Government would like Canadians and our creators to believe. The Government needs to take another concrete measure to provide for these creators. It requires the collective will of a number of different Ministers around the cabinet table. It takes directing the Ministers to be responsive to the needs of creators who enrich our lives and define us as Canadians, particularly in the following areas.
I refer to the definition of professional artist or professional artistic activity in the Income Tax Act; the erosion of Interpretation Bulletin IT-504; the establishment of a charitable or similar registered tax status of arts service organizations; specific aspects of the capital cost allowance deduction for the cost of musical instruments; and erosion of the capital cost allowance for investment in certified Canadian films. These are the kinds of additional measures that we need to ensure artistic creativity as an economic right in Canada.
Since the 1924 Copyright Act was passed there have been amendments. But, this is the first time that substantial revision has taken place. Every time the topic of copyright is opened up, a bell sounds and sides seem to be drawn. The Government thought that it had arrived at the perfect solution of having the copyright revision passed by introducing the amendments in two phases.
On May 28, the Government introduced this Bill, Bill C-60, supposedly the non-controversial part. It was to be the part that would be easy, acceptable and have an easy run through the House. Initially, the Bill received positive acclaim. I ask Hon. Members to remember the headlines. They read: "New Changes Would Give Copyright Laws More Teeth"; "Canada's Beefing Up Its Copyright and Royalty laws"; "Copyright Changes Applauded;" and "Copyright Bill-Good First Step". There certainly had been enough consultation. I refer to the White Paper entitled Gutenberg to Telidon; the 1985 subcommittee report entitled The Charter of Rights for Creators', and the 1986 Government response.
However, when Bill C-60 in its legislative form received second reading in this Chamber in June some minor technical changes were suggested, but that was all. It then went off to a legislative committee for hearings and quick passage into law. It was even suggested by government Members and my colleague from the New Democratic Party that hearings would not be necessary since all the issues had been covered.
Then came the lazy, hazy, crazy days of summer. Creators, users and copyright lawyers, instead of lolling on the beach or swimming, had to look much more closely at this Bill, for it is a very complex law. There is a great deal of legal jurisprudence through court decisions which had to be taken into consideration. They examined not only the changes in the Bill clause by clause, line by line, but word by word. They began writing letters and briefs, making phone calls and requesting meetings with Members to express their very serious concerns. They made constructive criticisms for improvement.
February 3, 1988

Letters and briefs to my office alone must have been very close to 300. Never before on a piece of legislation have I had to deal with such concerned feedback. It is feedback for which we should all be very grateful.
By October, when the legislative committee began its hearings, witnesses came before us. Some came with briefs requesting as many as 50 amendments. We were told by one witness that there were 75 places where there appeared to be differences from the drafting of the English and the French texts. It was sloppy work.
The Canadian Bar Association and the Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada appeared before us with a delegation of 12 lawyers and a 50-page brief. Some 50 concerns were examined. Their efforts represented the work of thousands of person hours. I was trying to calculate the amount of dollars that represented, but I gave up. This work was of tremendous value to the Minister, the Ministry, to the Opposition Parties, the people of Canada and to the whole legislative process. The comments presented by many of the witnesses and through the briefs were contradictory nonetheless. There was great division of opinion. As a matter of fact, it made for a very difficult hearing session.
During those hearings I began to wonder if the committee should not send the Bill back for a complete redrafting. However, I was convinced and hopeful that we would find the kinds of changes that would make this a fair, even and balanced Bill.
We were of the view that, through amendments, the concerns could be addressed. Thus we pressed and we did get substantial amendments made to Bill C-60. We should all be aware that that did take place. For that reason I would like to take this opportunity to thank all those who took the time to write letters and briefs, to phone and to appear as witnesses before the committee, answering countless questions, writing back, meeting with the Minister and both the Ministries of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Communications.
These people were very patient. All of us are indebted to them. I am also indebted personally, as I think the committee as a whole is, to the Library of Parliament staff whose members spent so many hours combing through the submissions to provide us with up-to-date analyses of the briefs, as well as preparing a comparative study of copyright laws in other countries, which proved very useful. It did not change the Minister's mind, but it was certainly a very useful exercise.
It was originally thought that this Bill would be the ideal solution and that copyright being divided into these two phases would be fine. We have now learned that there will probably be three phases.
Bill C-60 has been properly described as a creators' Bill, which has caused unease among the consumers of copyright such as libraries, schools and broadcasters, just to name a few. They had the right to express their points of view. They had the right to get together and to send in thousands of letters to
Copyright Act
all the Members of the House. I do not think that they should be criticized. They should be complimented for undertaking concrete concerned action in the interests of their constituencies. It was our responsibility to respond to those concerns, not to criticize them, as was done in a number of instances.
They have been told repeatedly that the exemptions will be in the next phase, which was their major area of concern. They want to know when the second phase will be. Will it be next week, next month or next year? The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) introduced this Bill on May 27. She said that the second phase would follow quickly in the fall. In December she said, "Come this spring". The spring has almost sprung and the grass has almost ris' and we still do not have hide nor hair of this Bill. The uncertainty causes concern and fear for the users. The representations brought me to the conclusion that the rights of users are inseparable from creators' rights. Many of their concerns are legitimate, for there is a lack of clarity and bridging has not been put into place. They are not sure about what they are going to find when the next part of this Bill comes in.
Copyright protection must be sufficient to stimulate and promote cultural and intellectual creation in Canada. The Social Science Federation pointed out in its brief "This cannot be achieved if the law fails to recognize the interests of cultural consumers who are equally vital to our cultural industries".
A real risk exists that new and powerful rights will be entrenched, and are being entrenched, without offsetting recognition and protection of legitimate concerns of the users of copyright material. After all, one would not buy a house without seeing all the rooms. Therefore, how would one expect users to be happy, satisfied, and support this legislation without seeing all the provisions? The Government has created unnecessary and undue concern which could have been avoided by having dealt with total revisions, or having released the second phase as draft legislation for both the users and the creators to be able to see the total picture.
The Communications Minister should have heeded the words of her colleague, or ex-colleague, the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who stated:
Copyright first of all protects creators, but consumers of their works are equally affected in their day-to-day life by the Copyright Act. Our legislation must ensure a balance between the interests of the copyright owner and the user.
I wish to address the education aspect, because we did hear from a large number of educators. There was much discussion during the legislative committee hearings on reprographic rights. The term "reprography" refers to the reproduction of a work specifically by photocopying. In today's society, we all take this act pretty much for granted.
Bill C-60 makes no substantive changes to the existing law insofar as photocopying practices are concerned. In the 1924

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
Copyright Act, under Section 3(1), the copyright owner has the sole right to reproduce the work or any substantial part thereof in any material form whatever. Accordingly, unless the reproduction is authorized by the creator or the copyright holder, and unless it is insubstantial or excused on the basis of any of the statutory exemptions under the current Act, the reproductions of a work by photocopying will be deemed to constitute a copyright infringement.
As for existing statutory exemptions that apply to photocopying practices, there are limited exemptions under Section 17(2)(h) of the 1924 Act for the reproduction of certain categories of protected works for their deposit under the Cultural Property Export and Import Act. It is too bad that we did not see fit to do that for the CRTC regulatory Act.
More important, there is the fair dealing limitation under Section 17(2)(a) which, by excusing "any fair dealing with any work for the purposes of private study, research, criticism, review, or newspaper summary;" may exonerate those who make photocopies, who are generally students, researchers, and many of us here in the House of Commons. They are exempted provided that they qualify under this limitation.
When the Canadian Teachers Federation representatives appeared before the legislative committee, they stated that they wanted the right to use material "spontaneously" in order to capture "the teachable moment". By this they meant the right to use new, timely, newsworthy copyrighted materials in a reasonable manner without the consent of the author. It would take too long and it would no longer be timely or of the moment. This, they define as "fair use". 1 think that that is fair play. This concept was accepted and incorporated in the 1976 revision of the United States copyright law. The American law provides recognition that fair use includes teaching, including multiple copies for classroom use; and a valid consideration as to "the purpose and character of the use".
For Canadian teachers the making of multiple copies, and particularly of current magazine articles, poems selected from books, and newspaper articles, has become a nearly entrenched practice. We were told by school boards that this situation has become even more important for teachers because of the cutbacks in educational funding that have occurred throughout Canada.
The educational community does not take the position that creators should not be recognized for the important contributions that they make in the creation of cultural works, and that creators are entitled to a reasonable return by way of royalties. There is no argument about that, and that is not the issue. Educators are concerned about having access to current materials when teaching such current topics as Meech Lake or free trade, materials that have not yet found their way into collectives; or that access to copyrighted materials will not be hamstrung in administrative procedures; and that costs will not be overbearing, making materials inaccessible.
Under Bill C-60, a legal foundation for the formation of "licensing bodies" has been established. Under licence
agreements negotiated on behalf of their members, the copyright owners, those organizations or collectives will be in a position to authorize the users to exercise the rights reserved exclusively to the copyright owners under the Act, such as the reproduction rights, thus providing the means by which otherwise infringing acts of photocopying can be legitimized.
In the background materials provided with Bill C-60, the Government uses the example of how collectives, creators, and schools operate in Quebec.

It is my "belle province", and I think it has shown real leadership in this respect.

In that province, the Quebec Ministry of Education signed agreements with I'Union des ecrivains du Quebec and the Society for the Advancement of Rights in Audiovisuals. Under those agreements, this enlightened procedure allows access to exactly the type of spontaneously used materials that we are referring to. The schools of Quebec have an immediate access repertory of literary and audio-visual works in exchange for $1.5 million a year which is negotiated with the Ministry of Education. As a result, creators are receiving payment while users have the immediate access that they need.
I would suggest that the Quebec example works well, and it is what the Government envisioned happening in the rest of the country. But it would appear that the Government failed in encouraging the relationship between the province and the collectives. As a result, educators and their students might well be the losers. I do not think that we want that. I am told that the provincial education ministries do not wish to proceed until they know what the exemptions are. Therefore, we are in a hang-up, not understanding the conundrum as to what this Bill really means. Teachers are worried, because teachers like to obey the laws of this land.
Bill C-60 does not assure that collectives will become a reality, nor does it mention the existence of "blanket licences". Quite to the contrary, it provides for individual bargaining between the user and the collective with only the limited jurisdiction of the copyright board.
It was out of those concerns that I proposed at report stage on Bill C-60 that the copyright board be able to make regulations governing "the spontaneous use for non-profit instructional purposes of works not included in a licensed repertoire". I included it in a section where they would be forced to consult with the Governor in Council in order that there would be no contradiction and we would be able to bridge phase one and phase two and make teachers comfortable that they were within the parameters of the law.
This amendment, if it had been accepted, would have allowed owners of copyright materials to rely on their rights to obtain compensation for the use of their works. It would have provided a mechanism for the resolution of disputes on the spontaneous use of copyright works. The copyright board, with
February 3, 1988

this amendment in place, would have had the authority that it needed, together with Governor in Council advice, to regulate the terms and conditions of spontaneous use and to fix any royalties associated with this use. The amendment would have referred to the board only those disputes pertaining to the use of material not included in the repertoire of the collectives.
I wish to look at broadcasters concerns. During the committee study of Bill C-60 we heard from broadcasters. They expressed concern that the area of ephemeral recordings had not been addressed by the Government. For the information of the House, an "ephemeral" recording refers to the practice of broadcasters of recording copyright material prior to transmission. It is an ongoing practice of all broadcasters, whether it is in the public or in the private sector. We are told that it is done for technical reasons. The recordings are often disposed of after being broadcast. Material is recorded because there is frequently a lag between the time that the program is produced and broadcast. Prerecordings allow broadcast at the desired date, time, and schedule. In a country with six time zones, it is necessary to meet time zone needs in various parts of the country. As you know, Mr. Speaker, they cannot exactly pull in an orchestra and do a live recording. They must have the right to record it and then rebroadcast it. The prerecording procedure allows networks to service various regions on a variable time schedule, which is normal practice.
It should be noted that the right to make an ephemeral recording does not itself create a right to broadcast the work that is recorded. It would still be necessary to obtain the authorization of the copyright owner to rebroadcast the work regardless of how long the ephemeral recording would be kept.
The current 1924 Copyright Act is totally silent on this exemption to allow such recordings in order to perform music which is already licensed by CAPAC and by PROCAN. Radio and TV broadcasters have been making convenience tapes for decades.
What will be the result for broadcasters of the Government ignoring the issue and not accepting my amendment? There are potential fines from $25,000 to $1 million, imprisonment for six months to five years, or both fines and imprisonment. The crime is the act of taping, without negotiating a mechanical fee with the publisher, music which they have been licensed to broadcast by CAPAC and PROCAN.
To add insult to injury, the situation only exists in Canada. It does not exist in the United States, Australia, or the United Kingdom. In their Copyright Acts they have an ephemeral right. To wait until the second phase is no excuse. It should have been in place, even on a temporary basis. If they put people outside the law, they cannot have much respect for government and laws.
In 1977 the Keyes-Brunet study on copyright in Canada recommended that ephemeral rights be included in new
Copyright Act
copyright legislation. They have certainly had enough notice. This is 1988 and that was 11 years ago.
A brief by the Canadian Music Publishers Association to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in 1979 recommended that ephemeral recordings should be dealt with in new legislation. In 1984 the Liberal Government released its White Paper and indicated its intention to provide an ephemeral exception in upcoming legislation. There were to be restrictions placed upon these exemptions, and those could have been addressed too. There was plenty of time to do that. The exemptions were the following: first, that the use of the copy was to be limited to the broadcasting organization for which it was intended; second, that all organizations concerned with broadcasting or the preparation of programs for broadcasting were to have the right to record agreed upon material for their own purposes, as long as the material was to be used solely for the agreed broadcasts; and, third, that the exemptions would also have applied when a broadcaster commissioned an independent producer to prepare a program.
In the charter of rights for creators it was also recommended that exemptions should be provided for the making of ephemeral recordings by broadcasters pursuant to existing CRTC regulations. They are in a position of jeopardy. They do not know whether they should agree and conform with the CRTC, go along with copyright, or face fines. It is a real dilemma. The second condition indicated in the charter would permit the broadcast of the program in a different time zone, provided that the recording is erased after eight days.
The Government agreed to the subcommittee's recommendations regarding ephemeral recording, but the Bill does not provide the necessary measures, leaving broadcasters in the same category as people who pirate and distribute records. 1 think that is reprehensible.
I have been advised that if the Government allows the present situation to stand, Canadian broadcasters will be faced with their greatest problem since 1929, when the Aird Commission recommended the abolishment of private broadcasting.
In respect of exhibition rights, Bill C-60 introduces those rights for the first time. The entrenchment of these rights into law was intended to provide much needed financial compensation for Canada's artists, but instead it has brought much unnecessary controversy and has created unfortunate tension between artists and museums.
The controversy began when the subcommittee on the revision of copyright not only recommended that a new copyright law should include exhibition rights but said:
-that a consensus has emerged in the artistic community on the recognition
of this new right.
Yet, no representatives from galleries or museums appeared before the subcommittee, while at least three associations on behalf of artists appeared. I do not think that is fairness or justice, and I do not think we were in a position to make the

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
wisest decision, not having had the benefit of these consultations.
I have said in the past that just because something is new is not a good enough reason not to accept it. Let us face the challenge of something new. I am not afraid of anything new, particularly if it has a potential to enable our artists to live more comfortably, if it has been subjected to some kind of testing or experience by which to evaluate such a right, and if there is consensus within the visual arts community about it.
Because I did not know very much about exhibition rights, I did some research. 1 found that no such right existed in Great Britain, Australia, or France. I also found a most intriguing situation in the United States which has the opposite effect to the proposed Canadian right. Under United States legislation copyright owners are vested with an exclusive right to display publicly a number of works, namely, literary, musical, dramatic and choreographic works, pantomimes, pictoral, graphic and sculptural works, and individual images of motion pictures and other audio-visual works.
However, a number of limitations are prescribed, the foremost of which is the one arising by virtue of the transfer of ownership of the work. Under this limitation, known as the first-sale doctrine, a person who lawfully acquires ownership of the work is entitled to display it publicly or authorize the public display of such a work without the copyright owner's consent.
If one buys such a work here but forgets to buy the exhibition rights, one can own it but never display it unless the artist agrees. One has to go back for permission time and again, and it is absolutely ludicrous. We must find a way to overcome that problem.
Accordingly, the owner of an original work of art in the United States is able to display it publicly in galleries, museums, shop windows, et cetera, without infringing copyright. In other words, he or she is permitted to do precisely what he or she will be prohibited from doing under the public exhibition right in Bill C-60 unless the copyright owner's consent is obtained.
I spoke earlier about division existing on exhibition rights in the artistic community. This division is not only between artists and museums but also among artists. Among the many letters I have received on exhibition rights, one artist wrote saying that exhibition rights "will not make my life worth living". She went on to say:
Although great for my ego, it does not match what happens in the marketplace. The Conservatives must come up with a more profitable solution, or be
more imaginative, to help my economics.
She went on to ask why should those who buy her pictures be restricted to where and when they show them, "for, after all, do you pay the dress designer every time you wear the dress?"
Museums and art galleries were concerned about the cost this new right might have, especially for smaller institutions
which the Canadian Museums Association said "are ill-equipped to bear the financial burden this will impose".
1 think we may well find a modus operandi, but we should have had dialogue to stop the potential conflict and incredible tension from building to this point.
The Government has implied that the placing of exhibit rights into law is only enshrining present practice. However, this is only partially correct. It is done by private contract. Most major public art galleries and museums voluntarily follow the exhibition fee schedule established by CARFAC, but the fee is applied only to temporary exhibitions which include loans from sources outside the permanent collection of the institution.
At the present time, institutions do not pay to exhibit works in their permanent collections which will not be the case after the passage of this Bill. That will place financial pressure on even major institutions. It was for these reasons that I suggested the Government would be better able to improve the status of the artist in Canada through the introduction of an exhibition right fund, as suggested by the Canadian Museums Association and the Professional Art Dealers Association of Canada. Such a fund would be similar to the Public Lending Rights Commission, a federally established fund administered through the Canada Council to compensate authors for the use of their books in public libraries. PADAC in its presentation to the committee said:
Such a fund would help to underscore the financial commitment of the
Government to support the arts in Canada, as well as provide a mechanism
that would relieve exhibiting institutions of the financial burden to pay these
fees.
These are the people who were involved in the whole issue both on the user and the consumer side. Instead, I think this right may have had the reverse effect of its intention. That is why I so dearly wanted us to have a review clause, in case there was a counter indication and we could then change or amend that provision.
Let us look at computer programs, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-60 will give computer software the same protection against illegal copying as has already been accorded to books. The Canadian software industry is worth about $1.5 billion and the industry estimates that illegal copying costs it close to $400 million a year, a lot of money. The legislation will give software copyright protection to authors for lifetime plus 50 years.
Bill C-60 as well increases the current $200 maximum penalty to $1 million or a five year prison term. Thus the Bill recommends penalties which will be effective deterrents. The legislative committee also amended the section dealing with computer programs to allow for the making of only one backup copy of a computer program. It was interesting that that exemption was allowed. It will not put computer companies into difficulty, but that exemption was not allowed for the broadcasting industry or the educators of this land.

I am, however, still disappointed that the Government has not taken action regarding semi-conductor chip protection. The United States has a Semi-Conduction Chip Protection Act which extends protection to chips created by Canadian nationals only if Canada enacts comparable legislation protecting chip originators. Canada has now been granted interim protection by the Americans. We should have done it for ourselves. The Bill was open, but we had to go to the Americans to get interim protection. I believe the Government would be best advised to give immediate and serious consideration to this issue. Since we do not have comparable legislation, the Canadian Government by its failure to act is placing Canadian semi-conductor chip originators at a serious disadvantage.
Let us take a moment and look at the mechanical royalty rate for composers. There exists, in the 1924 Copyright Act, a provision for compulsory licensing of mechanical reproductions which is a 2 cent rate for composers and music publishers of recorded music. It was intended for piano rolls-I do not know if you remember piano rolls, Mr. Speaker, I don't-and shellacked 78 RPM breakable recordings, those I do remember.
Oh, oh!

The law was passed in the heyday of silent pictures and three years before the first national radio broadcast. A year ago I called for the abolition of this section and, therefore, I am pleased to see the repeal of Section 19 for it has been 2 cents for too long.
During committee hearings we learned that under another clause compulsory licensing had been re-introduced. The legislative committee, however, I am pleased to say, deleted the objectionable clause. I greatly appreciate the Minister's move in that regard.
I am very worried about the retroactivity in the Bill. I think it is unconscionable and it goes against all the natural, normal democratic freedoms and rights that one would expect in a country of this kind. I am most disappointed that the Government chose not to accept my amendment calling for review of copyright on a continuing basis.
When Bill C-60 was introduced last June it was considered uncontroversial. It was even suggested that it would be the perfect Bill. However, as I have outlined, it is certainly not that. This Bill contains those new provisions about which I have spoken, exhibit rights, the introduction of collectives into new areas other than performing rights, the expansion of moral rights and the defining of computer programs as literary works. Because there is no experience, because of the interrelationship or interfacing with the Industrial Design Act, I believe that we should have a five year review. We would be in a better position to know whether the concerns expressed before our committee in 1987 are still concerns and remedial action need be taken. We do not wish to get into a situation of not attending to a Bill for 60 years.

I spoke about retroactivity and I have referred to many other aspects of this Bill. I would suggest that there is clear reason for concern. I think it has been unwise of the Minister not to react, particularly to that section. I believe it to be grossly unfair.
In closing my remarks, I am, nonetheless, pleased that the copyright Bill is in the process of amendment. I am hopeful that phase two will be in very quickly so that we can answer to the ongoing concerns of the users as well as the creators and find that Canadian way, that fairness, that balance that makes Canada such a special country, which should make this Act one of the most modern around the world. At this particular moment the revisions are not revisions of which we can be most proud.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to congratulate my friend, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) for her presentations today and the tremendous amount of work that she has done on this legislation. I want to recognize also the work done by my friend, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), as well as our critic, the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong).
It is time for this Bill because we have waited many years for it. I might say that we have waited since 1924 for legislation to be updated and passed. I suppose a bit of recognition ought to go to the Government for bringing this Bill forward and taking the initiative, a compliment that I sometimes find difficult to give.
Earlier today it appeared to me for a variety of reasons that it might be difficult to conclude third reading today, but that is not the case. I think sufficient discussions have taken place to complete third reading stage of this Bill.
Right from the beginning Members of the New Democratic Party have said that we want to expedite the passage of this legislation. It was long overdue. Creators have waited for a long time to see this Bill introduced and passed. It has been a disappointment for so many of our creators that they had to work with legislation passed some 60 years ago, especially when you consider the technological changes that have taken place in the cultural market-place so to speak.
At the time when this legislation was first passed there were no computers, no software or hardware for the computers, no television sets, no video cassettes only things like piano rolls and so on which my friend from Mount Royal indicated earlier with which some of us are familiar even to this day. The major changes that have taken place in artistic expression, dance and choreography obviously were necessary. Choreography used to mean the explanation of a theme or a story whereas today there is form choreography without a story. The legislation must be amended to include this new type of expression.

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
The new legislation provides for many, many other changes as well. I think we have heard enough of the details of them. 1 simply want to make some general comments at this final stage of debate.
This Bill provides us with two kinds of protection for creators, those people who express themselves artistically and make Canada the kind of unique place it is. The cultural community enables us to express ourselves as Canadians in a whole variety of forms using a whole variety of different media. That is what enables us to get a sense of ourselves, to create a Canadian personality and a regional personality.
The first protection Bill C-60 provides is related to economic rights. These are the rights that allow an artist to make a living and provide the creators of Canada with the legal authority to negotiate a royalty payment in return for permission to do any of the things only the creator of the work has the legal right to do. An example of this is the right to reproduce a work. This work may be sold to those who want to make copies of the work, and in this way, the Copyright Act provides the creator with the legal right to exploit his or her work in the market-place.
We have all heard different representations on the real meaning of giving creators their right to have their works recognized in the Copyright Act. I recall hearing an inquiry made by the trustees' association claiming that teachers would be breaking the law if they were to copy materials for spontaneous use in the classroom. 1 want to go on record as saying that the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) made it perfectly clear that these fears were unfounded. She insisted at the legislative hearing that Bill C-60 does not change the existing right regarding copying by students, teachers and librarians for spontaneous instructional purposes.
I believe we can clearly set aside that concern of so many people.
A second right of protection as provided by this Act relates to moral rights. The purpose of these rights is to protect the honour and reputation of the creators themselves. These rights therefore are personal. They are exercised by creators and may not be sold like economic rights. They may be exercised even with respect to a work whose economic rights have been sold and thus they add an extra layer of protection to a work a creator has already sold.
Bill C-60 also seeks to enhance the legal protection of visual artists for both moral and economic rights. A new economic right governing the exhibition of artistic works is provided in Bill C-60. On the moral rights front, the need to prove prejudice to honour and reputation has been removed and the remedies available for moral rights infringement have been
expanded. This must be excellent news for those we generally refer to as the creators.
When Bill C-60 was first tabled in the Elouse, my hon. friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood indicated that we welcomed this legislation and that we as a Party were keen to get it through the legislative committee because artists deserve this piece of legislation. She indicated at that time that our Party would co-operate by seeing that this Bill gets rapid passage. In that spirit, I would like to conclude my remarks. There is so much more I would like to say, but considering the need to pass this legislation and get on with things, I think it is only appropriate that I conclude now.
I would like to indicate an appreciation for the opportunity to say a few words on this. I look forward to hearing some comforting remarks from the Parliamentary Secretary aimed particularly at those who are students, teachers and librarians and use copyrighted material for spontaneous instructional purposes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, let me congratulate the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) and the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for their keen interest and hard work on the legislative committee which dealt with Bill C-60. The number of hours we have worked at this Bill is substantial. Their input has been greatly appreciated by the Government.
I would also like to thank the House Leader of the New Democratic Party for his intervention, understanding that he has some concerns about the Bill. I know that these concerns have been responded to.
I think all Hon. Members recognize how necessary it is to revise the existing law and how urgent it is to Canada's sense of cultural and intellectual independence to underline and affirm the legal, moral and economic rights of Canada's creative community. After more than 60 years of increasing social, economic and technological change, the watchdog over these rights, our original Copyright Act, had become an animal with little bark and even less bite. This has been made clear to all Parliamentarians and to the Canadian public throught the excellent work some two years ago of the subcommittee on the revision of copyright.
There is no question that the subcommittee's work and findings gave Government the impetus to undertake the revision we now debate. However, it did more than that. The subcommittee also gave encouragement to the creative community that this time those revisions would indeed become a reality. In 1985, the subcommittee's work was as thorough as it was extensive. In 1987, the legislative committee's work has been no less.

February 3, 1988

I believe that in the course of the last few months, the committee has heard or accepted some 100 briefs from individuals and organizations concerned or affected by the changes proposed in Bill C-60. I know that the Minister would want me to congratulate the members of the committee for both the time and the dedicated study they have given to these submissions. As a result of that work, a number of necessary amendments to the legislation have been adopted, amendments which 1 believe strengthen the principles of the Bill even further.	.
in this regard, I should like to note first the amendment to exhibition rights designed to exclude the display of certain works such as maps, plans and charts from this category. This material may have artistic as well as technical merit, but these works are not works of fine art for which the exhibition right was intended.
The second amendment I would like to mention is the one which more clearly defines what is and what is not a collective. Concern was expressed that the term "licensing body" as used in the Bill would apply to such organizations as film distributors and music publishers. Clearly, it was never the intention to consider such bodies as collectives. The definition of licensing body has been reworked, therefore, so that it does indeed encompass only true collectives.
There is one other amendment I should like to mention today, perhaps the most important one from the point of view of creators' rights. As Bill C-60 was originally drafted, there was a provision which in essence could have prevented a creator from withdrawing his or her work from public access on the expiration of a particular licence. It is certainly not the intention of Bill C-60 to impose arbitrary or compulsory restrictions on the creators' rights. It is the exact opposite. We have, therefore, amended the Bill to correct this anomaly.
I would like to add a word or two about exceptions. Some would have liked to see exceptions dealt with through amendments to Bill C-60. I know the Hon. Member for Mount Royal has expressed this view. It has been explained to members of the committee and the House why this issue must wait until phase two of copyright revision.
However, I must assure the House that the Minister is not unreceptive to the argument that there should be some exceptions, possibly for the disabled, for archives, or for music during religious services to name a few. The Government will, of course, look closely at every claim for exception. Until phase two is implemented, existing exceptions under current law will be maintained.
Copyright Act
However, there will have to be public policy incentives to justify an exception to a creator's exclusive rights to the use of his or her other works. Mere inconvenience or desire to save time or money do not provide such incentive.
Now that we have concluded report stage, it is the Government's hope that final passage of the Bill into law will be swiftly achieved.
[ Translation]
It is becoming increasingly urgent to adopt Bill C-60. If this legislation is not passed, innovative high-tech industries will be denied the kind of protection that would encourage their growth and development here in Canada.

We simply cannot afford to lose our best and most enterprising minds in the field of computer software, to take but the most obvious example, because they cannot be assured adequate protection of their work in their own country.
It is no less important to protect our artistic and cultural creators whose work is, in a very real sense, the soul of this great country. They must have the right to control and protect that which they themselves have created, whether the written word, a painting, a musical composition, a choreographed sequence of dance, or any of the other arts covered within the Bill. For example, abolition of the compulsory licence for the making of sound recordings will permit composers to control subsequent recordings of their music. They must be adequately compensated for use of their creations. This is no more, no less, than simple justice.
As the Minister has said to the legislative committee, we acknowledge that the Bill cannot satisfy everyone's demands. Some creators still believe it does not go far enough in enshrining into law the rights which should go with creation. Some users still believe it will place upon them excessive demands, both in administration and cost, which will only serve to limit public access to these works.
However, in reviewing the principles and mechanisms proposed within the Bill I do believe we have before us a workable and affordable system which will meet the major demands for copyright protection and compensation while at the same time ensuring affordable public access. Indeed, that access may even be enhanced.
Bill C-60 is also about incentive-incentive, in the case of software producers, to remain and create here in Canada; incentive, in the case of artists, writers, publishers, perhaps our academic institutions, our public libraries and galleries as well, to join in creating new works and new means of distributing them. This can only bring benefit and reward to all those who share the Government's belief that Canada's national identity,

February 3, 1988
Copyright Act
our sovereignty itself, depends upon our continuing cultural development.
[ Translation]
It is because of our faith in this development that we have decided to proceed with copyright reform. In some cases, we have followed the example of others and taken advantage of their experience. In other cases, we are setting an example for others.

In all cases we have endeavoured to respond to Canadian needs with provisions tailored to meet those needs. To the degree that Bill C-60 has received broad and continuing support from members of all Parties, 1 believe we have succeeded.
On a personal note, Mr. Speaker, this is my first experience in the legislative process as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications. It has been a great learning experience if one measures it in hours. This Bill has required a great many hours of work and much intervention.
In closing I would like to thank the House Leader for the New Democratic Party and the Hon. Member for Mount Royal for her interventions today and throughout the process. She has worked many hours as well, as has her research staff. I would also like to thank the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood who, at the initial stages, was involved very heavily, as was the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). We thank those people and congratulate them for their interventions.
I ask that our colleagues join myself, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal, the House Leader of the NDP, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood, and the Member for Regina East, to ensure the swift passage and speedy adoption of Bill C-60 into law.
The Hon. House Leader has indicated that we are now ready to proceed with the vote on third reading. This has been a very profitable experience and I thank all those who were involved. I understood there may be a question and I am prepared to answer any questions.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a point to which the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has not alluded. We have heard of the concerns of educators with regard to spontaneous copying such as writing poems on the blackboard.
I have received representation on an area which is of great concern to some librarians in this country, particularly those from academic and research libraries, who wish to make material available to other libraries in order to provide equal access to all academic resources for which there are numerous requests every day. Some very expensive books are available only in large libraries.
Would the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary advise whether the rather stiff penalties in the legislation before us would affect the existing practice of photocopying single copies of
articles of an academic or scientific nature for inter-library loans? Will this Bill affect that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the best way to answer the question of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) would be to refer him to the Minister's own words in the legislative committee. In order to make the issue quite clear she indicated that the fines and penalties apply only to commercial dealings in infringing copies, dealings about which the Act is very specific; selling, hiring, exposing for sale or hire and so forth.
I think the Minister's statement in the legislative committee answers the first part of the question. Nevertheless, people must remember that unlicensed copying is illegal. That is the law as it stands in the Act of 1924. Unlicensed copying is illegal. This does not change with Bill C-60. However, as I have pointed out from the words of the Minister in the legislative committee, fines and penalties apply only to commercial dealings in infringing copies.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that through legislation many other countries including Great Britain and the United States exempt single copies of academic and scientific papers for inter-library loan purposes from the copyright legislation. Could the Parliamentary Secretary indicate whether the Government is actively considering such an exemption?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I thank the Member for his question. The first objective of the Government was to establish the rights of creators in law. That is the process we have gone through. I am sure the Hon. Member has received the concerns he has just expressed from his constituents. We propose to deal with those concerns in phase two of the Bill which will allow for certain exemptions.
I think it is fair to say that the creators are not asking for the moon but simply for a certain respect for their talents, their skills, their efforts and respect for the right to have a say in and compensation from the use of their works. I do not think anyone would disagree or say that that is unreasonable.
I believe we are making an investment through Bill C-60. It is a modest investment when we consider the examples of those who have preceded us in that regard. The return will be an increase in creativity.
I believe the concerns about exemptions and exceptions will be dealt with fairly. The Minister indicated at the legislative committee that she is prepared to proceed as expeditiously as possible with phase two so that there will not be another wait of 60 years. She made the commitment at legislative committee to do this as quickly as possible and hopefully see phase two introduced in the House of Commons before the end of June.
February 3, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary is knowledgeable in the area. What will happen to our public and private broadcasters between phase one and phase two? Are they subject to fines and jail sentences because they will be following normal practice and complying with the CRTC regulations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two points to which the Hon. Member alludes. One is the timing and what will happen in the interim. I think I must refer to the second point first, concerning some of the cases that are pending with regard to other parts of the legislation, such as design. Currently, there are cases on design before the court. Clearly, if it infringes upon the rights of the creators as expressed in this law, they will be in contravention of the law as 1 understand it.
I repeat that it would be selling, hiring, exposing for sale or hire and so forth in that area. I think that answers her question.
